# m19-l03 narration (generated from the outline; do not edit)

## Slide 1

A River Model.

A mountain river models a circuit: the drop in height is like potential difference, and the water flow is like current.

Our big question for this lesson: how can you build a simple circuit to fit the needs of a given situation? Let's start with a mountain river, like the one in Figure 18. From its source high in the mountains, the river flows down to the plains. No matter which path it takes, its total drop in elevation is the same. Some rivers flow in a single stream, and others split into several smaller streams over waterfalls and rapids. Still, the total amount of water flowing down the mountain doesn't change.

Here's how the model maps onto a circuit. The distance the river drops is like the potential difference. The rate of water flow is like the current. Big rocks and other obstacles resist the flow, just like resistors.

So what plays the role of the battery or generator? The Sun! Solar energy evaporates water from lakes and seas, forming clouds that drop rain and snow on the mountaintops. Keep this river in mind as you read on.

## Slide 3

Series Circuits, Three Predictions.

Before closing a circuit, predict how bright two identical lamps in a single loop will be.

Three students connect two identical lamps to a battery, as in Figure 19. Before they make the last connection, their teacher asks them to predict how bright each lamp will be.

The first student predicts that only the lamp closest to the positive terminal will light, because all the current gets used up as light. The second student predicts that only part of the current gets used up, so the second lamp will glow, but more dimly. The third student predicts equal brightness. Why? Current is a flow of charge, and the charge leaving the first lamp has nowhere to go except through the second lamp. Same current, same brightness. Who do you think is right?

## Slide 4

Current in a Series Circuit.

A series circuit is a circuit with only one path for the current.

Think about the river model, and you'll see the third student is right. Charge can't be created or destroyed. With only one path to follow, the same amount of charge that enters the first lamp must leave it. The current is the same everywhere in the circuit.

Connect three ammeters around the loop, as in Figure 20, and they all show the same current. A circuit like this, with only one path for the current, is called a series circuit.

## Slide 5

Where Does the Energy Come From?

A lamp converts energy because there is a potential difference across it, delta V equals I times R.

If the current doesn't drop as it passes through a lamp, where does the energy to light it come from? The first two students were thinking about energy, and it made sense to them that current would shrink as electrical energy became light.

Remember, power, the rate at which electrical energy is converted, is P equals I times delta V. Energy conversions depend on both current and potential difference. Since the current doesn't change, there must be a potential difference across the lamp. The lamp's resistance is R equals delta V over I, so the potential difference across it is delta V equals I times R.

Curious about who designs circuits like these? Electrical engineers help design and develop electrical devices, from electric motors to power generation systems. They test those devices and make sure they work safely and efficiently.

## Slide 6

Equivalent Resistance in Series.

The equivalent resistance of resistors in series equals the sum of the individual resistances, R equals R one plus R two plus and so on.

In the river model, the height of the mountain equals the total drop the water makes on its way to sea level. In a circuit, the potential difference across the source equals the sum of the potential differences across the lamps: delta V source equals delta V one plus delta V two.

Since the current is the same through both, delta V one is I times R one, and delta V two is I times R two. So delta V source equals I times the quantity R one plus R two, and the current is delta V source divided by the quantity R one plus R two.

This works for any number of resistors in series. A single resistor that gives the same current is the equivalent resistance, and in series it's just the sum: R equals R one plus R two plus and so on. That's bigger than any single resistor, so with the same battery, adding more devices in series always lowers the current. To find the current, find R first, then use I equals delta V source divided by R.

## Slide 7

Voltage Dividers.

A voltage divider is a series circuit that produces a potential difference smaller than the battery's.

Suppose you have a 9-volt battery, but your circuit needs 5 volts. You can use a voltage divider, a series circuit that produces a smaller potential difference than the battery provides.

In Figure 21, two resistors, R one and R two, are in series across a battery with potential difference delta V. The equivalent resistance is R one plus R two, so the current is delta V divided by the quantity R one plus R two. The voltage you want is the drop across R two, which is I times R two. Substituting, delta V two equals delta V times R two, divided by the quantity R one plus R two.

Notice the current arrow in the diagram: it points away from the battery's positive terminal, because conventional current flows from the positive terminal, through the resistors, and back to the negative terminal. Pick the right pair of resistors, and you can get 5 volts out of a 9-volt battery.

## Slide 8

Photoresistors and Light Meters.

A photoresistor is a sensor whose resistance depends on how much light strikes it.

Voltage dividers often team up with sensors, like photoresistors. A photoresistor's resistance depends on the light hitting it. A typical one has about 400 ohms in the light, but about 400,000 ohms in the dark! So the output voltage of a voltage divider with a photoresistor depends on how much light is striking it.

That makes a handy light meter, like the one photographers use in Figure 22. An electronic circuit detects the potential difference and converts it to a measurement of illuminance on the digital display.

## Slide 9

Example Problem 4, Potential Difference in a Series Circuit (Part 1).

In series, I equals delta V source divided by the quantity R one plus R two, and delta V equals I R for each resistor.

Two resistors, 47 ohms and 82 ohms, are connected in series across a 45-volt battery. What's the current? What's the potential difference across each resistor? If we swap the 47-ohm resistor for a 39-ohm one, does the current go up, down, or stay the same? And what's the new potential difference across the 82-ohm resistor?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the schematic. Known: delta V source is 45 volts, R one is 47 ohms, and R two is 82 ohms. Unknown: I, delta V one, and delta V two.

Step two: solve. To get the current, first find the equivalent resistance, R one plus R two. Then I equals 45 volts divided by the sum of 47 ohms and 82 ohms, which is 0.35 amperes. Now use delta V equals I R for each resistor. Delta V one is 0.35 amperes times 47 ohms, or 16 volts. Delta V two is 0.35 amperes times 82 ohms, or 29 volts.

## Slide 10

Example Problem 4, Potential Difference in a Series Circuit (Part 2).

A smaller resistor in series lowers the equivalent resistance, so the current rises.

Part three: calculate the current again with 39 ohms as R one. I equals 45 volts divided by the sum of 39 ohms and 82 ohms, which is 0.37 amperes. The current will increase.

Part four: the new voltage drop across R two is 0.37 amperes times 82 ohms, which is 3.0 times ten to the first volts, or 30 volts.

Step three: evaluate. Current is measured in amperes, which are volts per ohm, and potential difference is measured in volts, which are amperes times ohms. Is the size realistic? The potential difference across any one resistor must be less than across the battery, and both delta V one and delta V two are less than 45 volts.

## Slide 11

Example Problem 5, Voltage Divider.

Delta V two equals delta V source times R two, divided by the quantity R one plus R two.

A 9.0-volt battery and two resistors, 390 ohms and 470 ohms, are connected as a voltage divider. What's the potential difference across the 470-ohm resistor?

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the battery and resistors in a series circuit. Known: delta V source is 9.0 volts, R one is 390 ohms, and R two is 470 ohms. Unknown: delta V two.

Step two: solve. R equals R one plus R two, and I equals delta V source over R. Then delta V two equals I times R two, which becomes delta V source times R two, divided by the quantity R one plus R two. Plug in: 9.0 volts times 470 ohms, divided by the sum of 390 ohms and 470 ohms, gives 4.9 volts.

Step three: evaluate. Volts times ohms over ohms leaves volts, so the units work. And the size makes sense: the answer is less than the battery's 9.0 volts, and since 470 ohms is more than half the equivalent resistance, the voltage across it is more than half of the battery's.

## Slide 12

Parallel Circuits.

A parallel circuit is a circuit with several current paths.

How many current paths do you see in Figure 23? The current from the generator can go through any of the three resistors. A circuit with several current paths is called a parallel circuit. The three resistors are connected in parallel, with both ends of all three paths joined together.

In the river model, that's three paths over a waterfall. Some carry lots of water, some just a little, but together they add up to the total flow over the falls. And whichever channel the water takes, it drops the same height. In the same way, in a parallel circuit the total current is the sum of the currents in each path, and the potential difference across each path is the same.

## Slide 13

Current in a Parallel Circuit.

Each branch current is I equals delta V divided by R, and the total current is the sum of the branch currents.

What's the current through each resistor in a parallel circuit? It depends on each resistance. In Figure 24, the potential difference across each resistor is 120 volts. The symbol V marks a voltmeter, which measures potential difference, and the symbol A marks an ammeter, which measures current.

Since I equals delta V over R, the current through the 24-ohm resistor is 120 volts divided by 24 ohms, or 5.0 amperes. The 9-ohm resistor carries about 13 amperes and the 6-ohm resistor carries 20 amperes. The total current through the generator is the sum of the three: 38 amperes.

## Slide 14

Changing a Parallel Circuit.

The branches of a parallel circuit are independent: removing one does not change the current in the others.

What happens if you remove the 6-ohm resistor from Figure 24? Does the current through the 24-ohm resistor change? No! That current depends on only two things: the resistance of that resistor and the potential difference across it. Neither changed, so its current stays the same. The same goes for the other branch.

The branches of a parallel circuit are independent of each other. But removing a resistor does lower the total current through the power source. Take out the 6-ohm resistor, and the total drops to 18 amperes.

## Slide 15

Equivalent Resistance in Parallel.

The reciprocal of the equivalent resistance equals the sum of the reciprocals of the individual resistances.

What single resistor would draw 38 amperes from a 120-volt source? R equals delta V over I, which is 120 volts divided by 38 amperes, or 3.2 ohms. That's smaller than any of the three resistors! Adding resistors in parallel always lowers the equivalent resistance, because each new resistor adds another path, increasing the total current while the potential difference stays the same.

To find the equivalent resistance, start with the total current: I equals I one plus I two plus I three. The potential difference across each resistor is the same, so each branch current is delta V divided by that resistance. That gives delta V over R equals delta V over R one, plus delta V over R two, plus delta V over R three.

Divide both sides by delta V and you get the rule: one over R equals one over R one, plus one over R two, plus one over R three, and so on for any number of resistors in parallel.

## Slide 16

Example Problem 6, Equivalent Resistance and Current in a Parallel Circuit.

In parallel, find each branch current with I equals delta V over R, then use one over R equals the sum of one over each resistance.

Three resistors, 60.0 ohms, 30.0 ohms, and 20.0 ohms, are connected in parallel across a 90.0-volt battery. Find the current through each branch, the equivalent resistance, and the current through the battery.

Step one: analyze and sketch. Draw the schematic, with ammeters showing where you'd measure each current. Known: R one is 60.0 ohms, R two is 30.0 ohms, R three is 20.0 ohms, and delta V is 90.0 volts. Unknown: I one, I two, I three, R, and I.

Step two: solve. The voltage across each resistor is the same, so use I equals delta V over R for each branch. I one is 90.0 volts over 60.0 ohms, or 1.50 amperes. I two is 90.0 volts over 30.0 ohms, or 3.00 amperes. I three is 90.0 volts over 20.0 ohms, or 4.50 amperes. Next, one over R equals one over 60.0 ohms, plus one over 30.0 ohms, plus one over 20.0 ohms, which is 0.100 per ohm, so R is 10.0 ohms. Finally, I equals 90.0 volts divided by 10.0 ohms, or 9.00 amperes.

Step three: evaluate. Current is in amperes and resistance in ohms. The equivalent resistance is less than any single resistor, the branch currents are inversely proportional to their resistances, and the total current equals I one plus I two plus I three.

## Slide 17

Kirchhoff's Loop Rule.

The loop rule: around any loop in a circuit, the sum of increases in electric potential equals the sum of decreases.

In 1845, when he was only 21, the German physicist Gustav Robert Kirchhoff came up with two rules for electric circuits: the loop rule and the junction rule. They help you analyze complicated circuits, and both rest on fundamental laws.

The loop rule is based on conservation of energy. Imagine hiking in a loop around the side of a hill, as in the top of Figure 25. You end where you started, so your final elevation equals your starting elevation. Every climb up is balanced by the climbs down.

Charges moving around a circuit loop do the same thing, except with electric potential instead of height. The sum of the increases in electric potential around any loop equals the sum of the decreases. That's conservation of energy: a charge that comes back to its starting point has the same potential energy it started with.

## Slide 18

Using the Loop Rule.

In a loop, the potential drop across the last resistor equals the battery's rise minus the other drops.

Look at the bottom of Figure 25. Picture a charge traveling clockwise around the red loop. Its electric potential rises by 9 volts going through the battery and drops by 5 volts going through resistor 1. What happens at resistor 2? The increases must equal the decreases, so the drop across resistor 2 must be 9 volts minus 5 volts, or 4 volts.

Notice that resistor 3 doesn't change our answer. Why? It isn't part of the loop with the battery, resistor 1, and resistor 2. In your own words, the loop rule says: go all the way around a loop, and every volt you gain, you lose again.

## Slide 19

Kirchhoff's Junction Rule.

The junction rule: the sum of currents entering a junction equals the sum of currents leaving it.

The loop rule is about potential differences and energy. The junction rule is about currents, and it's based on conservation of charge. Charge can't be created or destroyed, so the total current flowing into any part of a circuit must equal the total current flowing out.

The circuit in Figure 26 has two junctions, points where three or more wires meet, at A and B. The current entering a junction must equal the current leaving it, or charge would pile up there. That's Kirchhoff's junction rule. At junction A, I one equals I two plus I three. At junction B, I two plus I three equals I one. So if I two is 0.3 amperes and I three is 0.7 amperes, then I one is 1.0 amperes.
